- **[Stage]** Crawling for AI model training differs from search crawling because training mainly needs a very large number of tokens, and it matters little which pages they come from.
  <br><sub>`D1-C425` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D1-C422](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google panelist said they were working on a set of crawler best practices and offering research, malware-scanning and privacy crawlers an exemption from following them, apparently because such crawlers sometimes need to ignore robots.txt or probe URLs that other crawlers would not touch (the reason is a best reading: the audio has 'don't need', which would not explain an exemption).
  <br><sub>`D1-C432` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D1-C433](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Log files alone cannot show crawl inefficiency because they do not reveal where Google's crawl limit for the site lies; many similar URLs being crawled may not matter if the site is nowhere near that limit.
  <br><sub>`D1-C442` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D1-C441](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Many crawling complaints that reach Google's crawling team turn out to be caused by a plugin, for example a WordPress calendar plugin that adds calendar parameters to the URLs of every post, page, category and tag page.
  <br><sub>`D1-C446` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D1-C539](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** To check that new content is crawled fast enough, Gary Illyes advised measuring the time between publishing a URL and Googlebot's first crawl of it: ideally it stays flat or falls, and only a rising trend calls for investigation.
  <br><sub>`D1-C467` · Day 1, Q&A (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Answers [D1-C465](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Extended by [D1-C543](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The first priority in Google's own site consolidation was to identify the popular URLs people care about and make sure the migration did not damage them.
  <br><sub>`D1-C478` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D1-C476](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google panelist said Apple offers a robots.txt control for Applebot similar to Google-Extended, so a site can allow Applebot for search while opting out of Apple's AI use.
  <br><sub>`D1-C487` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D1-C481](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Repeated by [D1-C524](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** When logs show an unknown crawler fetching a lot, search for its user agent online to find the robots.txt token that controls it; the mainstream crawlers that send the most traffic can all be controlled this way.
  <br><sub>`D1-C488` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D1-C481](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google panelist said, as a fun fact, that JavaScript was used for the language-consolidation redirects in Google's own site migration, because it was the only option available to the person doing it (the recording does not make fully clear whether the JavaScript performed the redirects or built the mapping).
  <br><sub>`D1-C541` · Day 1, Q&A (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C479](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Extended by [D1-C542](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-CAN-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said that if the time from publishing to Googlebot's first crawl starts rising, how much it rises matters: for the crawling of fresh stories, something like two hours is probably not great (a smaller example figure is unclear in the recording).
  <br><sub>`D1-C543` · Day 1, Q&A (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C467](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Check and focus on rich results for Google.
  <br><sub>`D1-C122` · Day 1, session not recorded · not in Google docs · Extended by [D2-C521](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md)</sub>

## Day 2 — Indexing (2026-10-01)

| Status | Claims | Meaning |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Confirmed | 153 | The documentation says the same thing |
| Consistent | 228 | The documentation supports it without stating it directly |
| Not in docs | 217 | Said or shown at the event, by Google or a community speaker, but not in Google's documentation |
| Not checkable | 132 | Nothing to verify: quotations, framing, agenda facts, audience questions, opinions |

### Said at the event but not in Google's documentation

These are the most valuable and the most fragile claims: quote them as "said at Search Central Live", not as documented policy.

- **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that good HTML sitemaps are hard to make for large sites.
  > "It's hard to make good HTML sitemaps for large sites."
  <br><sub>`D2-C002` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C001](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that whether to keep a temporarily out-of-stock product page or redirect it depends on how important that product page is to users.
  > "It depends on the importance of the PDPs to the users."
  <br><sub>`D2-C010` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C009](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C841](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-ERR-04`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google answered on a Q&A slide that it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as a noindex because some extremely important sites disallow their most important pages, by accident or out of ignorance.
  > "Simply put, it's because of sites that are extremely important and like to disallow their most important pages, either accidentally or out of ignorance."
  <br><sub>`D2-C020` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (Gary Illyes, Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C019](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D1-C110](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extended by [D2-C844](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google contrasted out-of-stock products a buyer will wait for, such as a rare watch battery that matters to them, with easily replaced products, such as a particular cheese, for which the buyer simply picks a similar product instead of waiting.
  <br><sub>`D2-C841` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C009](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D2-C010](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google illustrated why it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as noindex with an extremely important site, such as a national tax authority, that blocks very important PDF files with robots.txt: Google cannot index the PDFs' content but can at least show their URLs in search results.
  <br><sub>`D2-C844` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · [Introduction to robots.txt](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) · Answers [D2-C019](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extends [D2-C020](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said very few URLs disallowed by robots.txt are in its index, compared with the index as a whole (no figure given).
  <br><sub>`D2-C845` · Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Answers [D2-C019](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Slide]** A Google slide titled Data from Crawling showed an example of what the crawler passes on for processing: the fetch result, the connect time and the time to first byte in milliseconds, the robots policies that apply to the fetch, and the raw HTTP response with the page's HTML.
  <br><sub>`D2-C024` · Day 2, How is HTML interpreted (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C063](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Extends [D1-C064](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Extends [D1-C092](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-PRF-01`</sub>

- **[Slide]** The HTML parsing step turns a fetched page's HTML into a Document Object Model (DOM) tree of elements, attributes and text nodes.
  <br><sub>`D2-C027` · Day 2, How is HTML interpreted (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-HTM-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The speaker said Google sometimes also extracts URLs that are typed out as plain text on a page without being hyperlinked; the remarks around this point were unclear in the recording.
  <br><sub>`D2-C046` · Day 2, How is HTML interpreted (Cherry Prommawin, Search Relations) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** A slide named internal admin pages, temporary landing pages and thin content as typical use cases for the noindex rule.
  <br><sub>`D2-C062` · Day 2, Controlling indexing (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** John Mueller said AI crawlers do not really know what to do with nofollow links, because they look at the content rather than building a link graph; he did not say whether he meant Google's AI systems, other AI crawlers or both.
  > "AI crawlers don't really know what to do with a nofollow link, because they're looking at the content"
  <br><sub>`D2-C066` · Day 2, Controlling indexing (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A max-snippet value too short for a useful snippet may lead Google to show no snippet at all, John Mueller said.
  <br><sub>`D2-C084` · Day 2, Controlling indexing (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-IDX-05`</sub>

- **[Slide]** max-snippet:-1 removes the length limit and can produce a longer snippet than having no rule, because by default Google keeps snippets to a length it considers reasonable instead of quoting a page at length.
  > "max-snippet:-1 = No limit. (can be more than without)"
  <br><sub>`D2-C085` · Day 2, Controlling indexing (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** John Mueller said Google Search does not always show an image thumbnail for a result, and when it does, the thumbnail is usually limited to the size of the result entry.
  <br><sub>`D2-C088` · Day 2, Controlling indexing (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** John Mueller's slide said Search Console has very few indexing-like settings and listed the Search generative AI control as the one control in his talk that is not a meta tag.
  > "Very few "indexing-like" settings are in Search Console"
  <br><sub>`D2-C102` · Day 2, Controlling indexing (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Compared with other search engines and AI crawlers, Google said its effort to mimic what the user sees is essential to keeping its knowledge of the web up to date and comprehensive; it did not say what the others do.
  <br><sub>`D2-C113` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Being able to render and read JavaScript matters whether the client fetching a page is a search crawler or an AI system, Google said.
  <br><sub>`D2-C114` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google described the mission of its rendering as simply executing JavaScript, while the implementation is complex, expensive and difficult.
  > "our mission is very simple these days: execute JavaScript"
  <br><sub>`D2-C115` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** To train Gemini models, Google renders every page just as it does for Search, so a page that renders correctly for Search also works for Gemini training, provided the site allows its content to be used for training.
  > "if it works for Search, it works for Gemini for training"
  <br><sub>`D2-C118` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C039](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** When a Gemini user asks about a specific web page (for example, whether it says anything about the ruby HTML tag), the page is read at that moment rather than during crawling and may be used to ground the answer, which takes extra time.
  <br><sub>`D2-C120` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C039](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by `DEV-PRF-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** After the crawler has fetched a page, Google's rendering system executes it, checks that it loads properly and works out what it looks like at different sizes.
  <br><sub>`D2-C129` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said its pipeline needs to ensure that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering, while content that appears only through JavaScript and CSS takes a longer rendering pass.
  <br><sub>`D2-C130` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Switching JavaScript off and on in the browser gives a quick first impression of which content on a page depends on rendering.
  <br><sub>`D2-C138` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Offer counts, discounts and other data should always be the same in the raw HTML and the rendered page, a community speaker advised.
  <br><sub>`D2-C147` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-REN-07`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A search engine's renderer does not wait forever before taking its snapshot, so content from slow internal systems or APIs can be missing and unresolved placeholders can end up in the final snapshot, a community speaker said.
  <br><sub>`D2-C149` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D2-C259](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) · Extended by [D2-C263](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Unresolved placeholders caused by rendering timeouts are hard to catch because the problem moves around: it is not always the same page that is broken.
  <br><sub>`D2-C151` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-MON-05`, `DEV-REN-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** To catch intermittent rendering problems, archive the full HTML and the resources of each page during a site audit and analyse them yourself, a community speaker advised.
  <br><sub>`D2-C153` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-MON-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Content Security Policy lowers the risk of cross-site scripting and clickjacking by defining trusted hosts; a resource from a host that is not trusted is not used.
  <br><sub>`D2-C155` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-REN-09`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A page can render completely blank while its raw HTML looks fine, so a team checking only the raw HTML thinks all is well; causes include server misconfiguration, overload and bad scripts.
  <br><sub>`D2-C159` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-MON-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker strongly advised SEOs to use Chrome DevTools more often to understand what happens when their pages render.
  <br><sub>`D2-C162` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D2-C860](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Third-party systems billed per session that also run when bots render a page can cost a high-traffic site thousands of euros per month, a community speaker said, adding that he sees this regularly.
  <br><sub>`D2-C163` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-PRF-03`</sub>

- **[Slide]** A community speaker's slide put the usual wait in Google's render queue at seconds to a couple of minutes per page.
  > "Usually from seconds to a couple minutes."
  <br><sub>`D2-C171` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** If a page keeps loading content indefinitely, not all of that content will be indexed, because Google's rendering does not go on forever (this passage of the recording is partly unclear).
  <br><sub>`D2-C175` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-REN-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** If content is missing from the rendered HTML, find the script responsible in Chrome DevTools: open the Network tab, filter by Fetch/XHR and reload the page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C180` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** If the cause of missing JavaScript content is still unclear after checking the network requests, search the source code for a string related to the missing content.
  <br><sub>`D2-C182` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Rebecca Yu) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Natalia Venditto named three typical failure modes by which an embedded app can break the application hosting it: collisions in the global JavaScript scope and module registry, CSS bleed, and fate sharing.
  <br><sub>`D2-C219` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** CSS bleed, as Natalia Venditto described it, means styles leak between an embedded app and its host, so that suddenly everything looks like the embedded app or the embedded app takes on the look of the host.
  <br><sub>`D2-C220` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Fate sharing means a failure in an embedded app spreads to its host, for example an unhandled exception in the embedded app that ends up breaking the host application.
  <br><sub>`D2-C221` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** An iframe, the long-established way to embed an app, isolates both JavaScript and styles but is not part of the page: it is walled off from the host's DOM, navigation and layout, which Natalia Venditto said brings many problems with accessibility, layout and navigation.
  > "Walled off from DOM, navigation, layout"
  <br><sub>`D2-C224` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Shadow DOM isolates styles and keeps the embedded content part of the page, but it does not isolate JavaScript: the embedded code still shares the host's JavaScript globals.
  > "Still shares JS globals"
  <br><sub>`D2-C228` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Shadow DOM*</sub>

- **[Slide]** Rewriting everything into one application keeps the result part of the page, but JavaScript and style isolation then have to be done by hand.
  <br><sub>`D2-C229` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Reframing with Web Fragments was the only approach on the comparison slide ticked for all three criteria (JavaScript isolated, styles isolated, part of the page); its stated catch is that it relies on browser patches today.
  > "Needs patches today"
  <br><sub>`D2-C231` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Web Fragments is a lightweight library that puts a hidden iframe in the host page and uses it as an isolated sandbox to run the embedded app's JavaScript, not to render the app.
  <br><sub>`D2-C232` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Web Fragments fetches the embedded app's assets from a remote endpoint through middleware that acts as a gateway.
  <br><sub>`D2-C233` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Web Fragments reframes the embedded app's DOM by placing it inside a shadow DOM in the host page, while the app's JavaScript runs in the hidden iframe.
  <br><sub>`D2-C234` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** With Web Fragments the page ends up as a single document in which the host application does not know the embedded app runs inside it and the embedded app does not know it lives in another document.
  <br><sub>`D2-C236` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Web Fragments monkey-patches browser APIs to containerize the browser, recreating inside it an architecture similar to Docker containers on the back end.
  > "we monkey patch the browser to containerize it"
  <br><sub>`D2-C237` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** The browser APIs Web Fragments patches include document, history and location; Natalia Venditto said they are virtualized rather than hijacked, so controls work exactly as in a normal application.
  <br><sub>`D2-C238` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Web Fragments retargets dispatchEvent calls to the fragment's shadow root and resolves DOM calls such as appendChild and element lookups against the main document.
  <br><sub>`D2-C239` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Natalia Venditto said Web Fragments suits AI-generated apps because a web fragment used as a custom element sandboxes the app's rendering, avoiding collisions and CSS bleed between the app and its host in either direction.
  <br><sub>`D2-C241` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** A slide set out Web Fragments in five steps: an LLM writes the app and adds a custom element such as `<web-fragment fragment-id="some-id">` to the HTML, a standalone HTTP endpoint is set up, the library is imported and initialized with initializeWebFragments(), the fragment is registered in the gateway, and step 5 is a celebration emoji.
  <br><sub>`D2-C242` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Natalia Venditto said the five Web Fragments steps are all that is needed to run a containerized application fully on the client side.
  <br><sub>`D2-C243` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** A web fragment is served from its own standalone HTTP endpoint, so the embedded app can be deployed anywhere, separately from the host page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C244` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Natalia Venditto said Web Fragments is framework-agnostic and vendor-agnostic and works the same whatever JavaScript framework the embedded app uses.
  <br><sub>`D2-C246` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Natalia Venditto reported an enormous performance increase (no figure given) when an application is reframed inside a fully client-side host, because the reframed app is rendered and interactive immediately.
  <br><sub>`D2-C248` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Natalia Venditto said a server-rendered app reframed into the host page is fully indexable.
  <br><sub>`D2-C249` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-REN-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Natalia Venditto said ShadowRealm, a JavaScript standard proposal, was at stage 2.7 at the time of the talk, which she glossed as meaning that only implementation is missing.
  > "the only thing missing is implementation"
  <br><sub>`D2-C253` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Natalia Venditto said the ShadowRealm proposal would do much of what Web Fragments does today with patches: containerizing and isolating execution.
  <br><sub>`D2-C254` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Natalia Venditto) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D2-C281](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Search engines such as Google and Bing would ignore HTML tags written inside a meta description, a community speaker said.
  <br><sub>`D2-C858` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C142](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-HTM-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Besides using Chrome DevTools more often, a community speaker advised checking rendering at scale with a modern crawler.
  <br><sub>`D2-C860` · Day 2, Lightning session D: Rendering and JavaScript (Sören Bendig) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C162](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-05`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's slide called content missing from the rendered HTML the most common JavaScript issue for indexing.
  > "The most common issue."
  <br><sub>`D2-C261` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-REN-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Content is missing from the rendered HTML either because the server does not serve it or because the content has still not appeared after some period of time.
  <br><sub>`D2-C263` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C149](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Instead of scrolling, Google renders a page in a very tall viewport, around 10,000 pixels high.
  > "it renders it in a very tall viewport. Specifically, around 10,000 pixels is what the viewport gets rendered as."
  <br><sub>`D2-C272` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C199](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) · Used by `DEV-REN-03`, `DEV-URL-07`, the glossary term *Viewport expansion*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Polyfills work in two directions: they patch backwards where a browser lacks support, or patch forward to build now for a feature expected in the future, as Web Fragments does.
  <br><sub>`D2-C281` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C254](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Erin Sparling called URL fragments (the part of a URL after #) the next most common JavaScript issue seen, after rendering problems and blocked rendering.
  <br><sub>`D2-C283` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Real URLs also work as deep links: Android, iOS and desktop operating systems accept full URLs as keys to specific content in an app, so clean URLs simplify the cross-platform user experience, not only indexing.
  <br><sub>`D2-C289` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-URL-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A headless content management system serves its content as an API; even WordPress, often seen as one monolithic application, can be used headless, with only its editor or only its renderer.
  <br><sub>`D2-C299` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Combining schema-based interfaces with web standards such as WebMCP lets a site expose tools to AI agents, which can then operate the interfaces, for example to test them.
  <br><sub>`D2-C303` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C281](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Erin Sparling showed a Search Console result saying a URL would be indexed only under certain conditions, one of which had not been met, and contrasted it with the result for an available URL whose content loads.
  <br><sub>`D2-C307` · Day 2, What is Google friendly JavaScript (Erin Sparling) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Words in the footer of a page get a lower weight, so text placed in the footer is unlikely to contribute much to ranking the page.
  > "if you put something in a footer, it's more likely that it's not going to contribute much to ranking"
  <br><sub>`D2-C313` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-HTM-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said not everything on a page can or should be important: if everything were placed in the main content, nothing would stand out as main content, which he called working as intended.
  <br><sub>`D2-C316` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google does not store the complete sentences or the full HTML of a page in the Search index, because large pieces of text would be unsearchable; it tokenizes the text into the smallest segments that still allow search.
  <br><sub>`D2-C318` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Repeated by [D2-C721](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Extended by [D3-C109](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) · Used by the glossary term *Tokenization*</sub>

- **[Stage]** For languages written with spaces between words, such as English and German, Search tokenization splits a sentence into its individual words.
  <br><sub>`D2-C319` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Text in languages written without spaces, such as Thai and Chinese, would end up in the index as long strings that might never be searched for, so Google segments it into words with statistical models built from other web content in that language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C320` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C011](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Repeated by [D3-C070](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For languages written without spaces, such as Thai and Chinese, Google uses exactly the same word segmentation when indexing a page as when interpreting the user's query, because otherwise the query could not be matched against the index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C321` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Repeated by [D2-C737](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Extended by [D3-C013](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** When tokenizing for Search, Google attaches metadata to each token for use in ranking, such as whether the word appeared in the header or in the main content (tagged 'centerpiece' on the slide), in bold or in a heading; Gary Illyes said he was not showing all of the metadata.
  <br><sub>`D2-C323` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Repeated by [D2-C720](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Used by `DEV-HTM-07`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google also stores spam metadata with the tokens of a page, for example that text was white on a white background, so ranking can use that information.
  <br><sub>`D2-C324` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-HTM-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Tokenization for AI models such as Gemini, in training and in inference, differs from tokenization for Search, although Gary Illyes qualified this with 'or mostly'.
  <br><sub>`D2-C325` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Contradicts [D1-C039](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's two tokenization slides showed the difference on the same sentence: the Search tokenizer kept 'robots.txt' and 'tl;dr' as single tokens, while the AI-model tokenizer split them into pieces such as 'tl' and 'dr' or 'robots' and 'txt', with the punctuation as separate tokens.
  <br><sub>`D2-C328` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes added that, once chunk size is thought of in millions of tokens as Gemini's context window allows, chunking has perhaps lost its meaning anyway.
  <br><sub>`D2-C825` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C332](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Because error pages are worded in endless variations, of which 'page not found' is only the classic one, Google cannot detect soft 404s with simple error, word or keyword matching.
  <br><sub>`D2-C335` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Mistakes in Google's own systems are a further cause of soft 404s, and Gary Illyes asked site owners to report such mistakes in Google's forums.
  > "BONUS: Mistakes in Google's systems (that you should notify us about)"
  <br><sub>`D2-C337` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google detects soft 404s with a language model, described as something like BERT, that is trained to understand the structure and layout of a page as well as its language, instead of reading the page as one flat wall of text.
  > "This is basically an LLM thing, something like BERT, that is specifically trained to understand page structure"
  <br><sub>`D2-C338` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C042](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For soft 404 detection, the position of error text decides: an error in a less important part such as the navigation need not make a page a soft 404, but an error message alone in the main content, like 'Error establishing a database connection', does, much as a human would judge it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C339` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C078](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) · Used by `DEV-ERR-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's soft 404 detection tells the page chrome, such as navigation and footer, apart from the main content by analysing the page's visual hierarchy alongside its text.
  <br><sub>`D2-C340` · Day 2, Understanding what's on a page (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Storage is a second reason for deduplication: Google's storage has many competing uses and storage prices have risen sharply, so the space for any one use is limited and Google has to draw a line somewhere.
  <br><sub>`D2-C350` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google clusters duplicate pages by content in four ways: exact matches, near matches, structurally similar content, and soft 404s.
  <br><sub>`D2-C364` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google sometimes picks a canonical that looks unrelated because it recognised a URL pattern: if /buy/fax, /buy/typewriter and /office-equipment show the same content, its systems may assume any /buy/ URL, even /buy/seo-service, shows that same office-equipment content without looking at the page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C368` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-CAN-08`, `DEV-URL-09`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's slide on structurally similar content asked whether a new URL that fits a known duplicate pattern, such as /buy/seo-service, even needs to be crawled.
  > "Do we even need to crawl /buy/seo-service ?"
  <br><sub>`D2-C369` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C128](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) · Extends [D1-C094](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-CAN-08`, `DEV-URL-09`</sub>

- **[Slide]** City pages can trigger the same pattern-based deduplication: for a car dealer brand with branches in several cities and similar stock, Google's systems may decide the city name does not matter and canonicalise to one city's page; the slide asked whether a further city page such as /zurich/services would be treated the same way.
  <br><sub>`D2-C370` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-CAN-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** AI agents that browse the web for users run into the same bot walls that sites put up against scrapers, and may give up and go to another site, for example to buy the product elsewhere.
  <br><sub>`D2-C377` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C436](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google picks the canonical from a variety of criteria and uses some kind of machine learning to decide how much weight each criterion gets; the weighting changes from time to time.
  > "we use some kind of machine learning to understand how strong these criteria should be. And this changes from time to time."
  <br><sub>`D2-C386` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's speaker said that pointing rel=canonical from the pages of a paginated set to the first page can sometimes make sense depending on the goal, for example to make a category page more visible, but that it affects canonicalization and deduplication.
  <br><sub>`D2-C393` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs · Contradicts [D1-C115](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-06`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's duplication talk closed with the advice not to block agents, which the speaker said are sometimes really cool.
  > "Don't block agents."
  <br><sub>`D2-C397` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C131](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's speaker suggested checking rel=canonical links with a crawler such as Screaming Frog to make sure they are reasonable.
  <br><sub>`D2-C398` · Day 2, Handling web duplication (John Mueller, Search Relations Team Lead) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D2-C408](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Canonical chains can run through canonical links alone, through a server-side redirect between members, or through a client-side redirect between members.
  <br><sub>`D2-C421` · Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves (Tobias Schwarz) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Canonical loops, such as two HTML pages whose canonical tags point to each other, are a structural conflict: the group has no canonical leader, so its canonical information cannot be used.
  <br><sub>`D2-C424` · Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves (Tobias Schwarz) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-CAN-04`, the glossary term *Canonical chain and canonical loop*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Canonical loops can also run through server-side or client-side redirects, not only through canonical tags.
  <br><sub>`D2-C425` · Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves (Tobias Schwarz) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said that at best a search engine's heuristic would treat a canonical loop through redirects as self-referencing canonicals, and doubted that this is often done when the loop runs through a client-side redirect.
  > "But regarding the client-side redirect, I highly doubt that this is often done."
  <br><sub>`D2-C426` · Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves (Tobias Schwarz) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker said pages carry different link equity, and a canonical leader that is not the strongest page in its group is technically valid but most likely suboptimal for ranking, so the strongest page should be the leader.
  <br><sub>`D2-C429` · Day 2, Lightning session E: Managing Duplicates and Site Moves (Tobias Schwarz) · not in Google docs · Contradicts [D2-C348](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's indexing pipeline slide put a Processing stage between the crawler and the index and listed HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication and feature extraction above it, with feature extraction highlighted as the step of this talk.
  <br><sub>`D2-C441` · Day 2, Finding the gold nuggets: structured data, media, and more! (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C063](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Repeats [D2-C026](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's indexing pipeline slide drew a feedback line from the Processing stage back to the crawl queue.
  <br><sub>`D2-C442` · Day 2, Finding the gold nuggets: structured data, media, and more! (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Repeats [D2-C048](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's indexing includes a dedicated system, whose internal name Gary Illyes would not disclose, that extracts the parts of a page that are traditionally expensive to extract.
  <br><sub>`D2-C443` · Day 2, Finding the gold nuggets: structured data, media, and more! (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google runs deduplication before feature extraction, so that the expensive extraction work is spent only on a trimmed-down, manageable set of documents.
  <br><sub>`D2-C444` · Day 2, Finding the gold nuggets: structured data, media, and more! (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C026](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Used by `DEV-SDA-10`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said feature extraction, which extracts page structures into a form Google's systems can consume internally, is still expensive, though not the most expensive operation.
  <br><sub>`D2-C449` · Day 2, Finding the gold nuggets: structured data, media, and more! (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** AI Overviews and AI Mode launched as fairly text-heavy answers with little image content and few tables, and they have become more structured over time because that is what users want.
  <br><sub>`D2-C453` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C011](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google gave four reasons why structured data is still valuable even though models can extract information from pages: precision, extra content, efficiency and focus.
  <br><sub>`D2-C458` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Structured data gives the high precision that complex schemas such as sale pricing need, with higher accuracy than large-scale extraction by large language models (LLMs).
  > "Structured data provides the high precision needed for complex schema (sale pricing), achieving higher accuracy than large-scale LLM extraction."
  <br><sub>`D2-C459` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** In the speaker's own tests, even the latest LLMs asked to generate schema.org markup for a page often invent properties that do not exist, get deeply nested schemas such as complex pricing models wrong, and duplicate content across several fields.
  <br><sub>`D2-C460` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Automatic LLM extraction of structured information makes a great demo but is not yet good enough for extraction that aims at something like 99.9% accuracy, the speaker said.
  <br><sub>`D2-C461` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Structured data often carries non-visible metadata that the page text lacks, such as full ISO dates or stable identifiers for user-generated content.
  > "It often contains non-visible metadata, such as full ISO dates or stable identifiers for UGC, that is not present in the page text."
  <br><sub>`D2-C463` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-04`, `DEV-SDA-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's own extraction systems focus heavily on what is visible on a page, which improves precision but means they can miss content or interpret it incorrectly.
  <br><sub>`D2-C464` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Parsing structured data is significantly cheaper and more efficient than relying on LLMs for every complex extraction task.
  <br><sub>`D2-C469` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Repeated by [D3-C405](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Even Google cannot afford to run complex AI models on every page in its index, and distilling them into cheaper models makes them less precise.
  <br><sub>`D2-C470` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Rule-based parsing of markup is nearly free by comparison with AI models, so Google will always prefer extracting information from structured data over model-based extraction.
  > "So we're always going to prefer that particular approach."
  <br><sub>`D2-C471` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Structured data explicitly points to the pertinent data on a page, which reduces noise and stops Google's systems from pulling in extraneous information such as prices of related products.
  <br><sub>`D2-C473` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-07`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's systems sometimes fail to determine a page's main content correctly, and structured data helps because site owners tend to mark up what is actually important rather than boilerplate or ads.
  <br><sub>`D2-C474` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C028](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Used by `DEV-SDA-07`</sub>

- **[Stage]** As far as the speaker knows, in most of Google's main AI uses a page's schema.org markup is not turned into text and put directly into the model's context; the data is first sorted out, checked for quality and indexed before it is passed on as grounding context.
  <br><sub>`D2-C477` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C061](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The speaker said there are concerns that feeding raw schema.org markup straight into an AI model's context would be a big abuse vector, one reason Google does not do so.
  <br><sub>`D2-C478` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Microdata has an advantage when payload size matters: embedded in the existing HTML, it avoids duplicating the page content in a separate JSON-LD block.
  <br><sub>`D2-C496` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-01`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Several plug-ins emitting the same markup type is one of the most common structured data problems: the duplicates can make an event details page look like a list of events and change how Google interprets the page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C503` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Schema.org, in which Google is a major participant, began publishing usage statistics for all its types and properties in 2026, showing in buckets how many domains use each one; the data is also in schema.org's GitHub repository.
  <br><sub>`D2-C510` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google often needs to see a markup type adopted on websites before it invests in a feature that uses it, a chicken-and-egg problem that the schema.org usage statistics are meant to help break.
  <br><sub>`D2-C511` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C120](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Schema.org added support for RDF lists and sets, which give a way to express ordered values, because RDF triples are not ordered by nature.
  <br><sub>`D2-C512` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google announced server-side structured data validation as coming soon: it will publish downloadable validation rules in SHACL on each structured data feature guide, with other kinds of checks to follow.
  <br><sub>`D2-C514` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-12`, the glossary term *SHACL*</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's planned validation workflow has five steps: download the rules from the feature guide, generate the JSON or embedded microdata or RDFa, run the rules against the generated server-side markup as a first check, deploy and test in the Rich Results Test, and monitor ongoing performance in Search Console.
  <br><sub>`D2-C515` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-12`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The SHACL rules are meant to run inside a site's content generation, so markup is sanity-checked before it is published and does not silently regress later, a breakage site owners might otherwise discover only through a Search Console report.
  <br><sub>`D2-C516` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-12`, the glossary term *SHACL*</sub>

- **[Stage]** The SHACL rules will not replace Search Console as the canonical place for structured data reports, because some checks use Google's internal libraries and cannot be expressed in SHACL, but they will catch problems such as a missing required field.
  <br><sub>`D2-C517` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-12`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google plans a SHACL rule set for each of its structured data feature types and will release the rule sets gradually once they have been checked.
  <br><sub>`D2-C519` · Day 2, What is Structured Data and why we need it on the internet. (Ryan Levering, Software Engineer) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-SDA-12`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes suggested a div with a CSS background image as a way to keep an image from being picked up by Google.
  <br><sub>`D2-C826` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-IMG-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Of the attributes the HTML standard defines for the img element, Google uses three and ignores the rest; Gary Illyes named src and alt but not the third.
  <br><sub>`D2-C531` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes ranked the alt attribute below src in importance, while saying alt attributes are still important.
  <br><sub>`D2-C533` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes cited a figure that more than 40% of Southeast Asian shoppers rely on videos to make purchase decisions.
  <br><sub>`D2-C546` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said over 219 million people in Southeast Asia consume content on or through YouTube daily (the daily scope was heard in two independent recordings but is not verified).
  <br><sub>`D2-C547` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said there are over 150 streaming apps in Southeast Asia.
  <br><sub>`D2-C548` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google knows from experiments that when a video's thumbnail is wrong, the share of viewers who drop out at the start of the video is extremely high.

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes called the 'fast-loading pages' factor for video SEO a misnomer: what matters is that the video itself loads fast, because people no longer have the patience to wait for videos to load.

- **[Stage]** Serving videos from a content delivery network (CDN) that loads them faster than the site's own server is a win for video SEO, Gary Illyes said.

- **[Stage]** Video sitemaps are not critical but good to have, because Google ingests video sitemaps much more often than it can process HTML pages.

- **[Stage]** Descriptive text around a video helps Google rank and retrieve the video.
  <br><sub>`D2-C927` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-VID-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The more people talk about a site's videos, the more likely Google is to surface them in search results, so videos should be promoted.
  <br><sub>`D2-C929` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's media indexer processes the images and videos that feature extraction passes to it and attaches them to the URL of the page that hosts them.
  <br><sub>`D2-C930` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C448](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Unlike a disallowed web page, whose bare URL can still appear in web results, a video blocked by robots.txt is not shown by its URL, because Google sees no good reason to show a video URL alone.

- **[Stage]** Gary Illyes said noimageindex also affects videos on the page, because Google has to index a video's thumbnail, which is an image.
  <br><sub>`D2-C935` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-IDX-09`, the glossary term *noimageindex*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google serves AI-generated images and videos in search results when users are specifically looking for them.
