  <br><sub>`D2-C938` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** The diffusion models that generate images were built to generate images, not text, so they are typically poor at rendering text inside an image.
  <br><sub>`D2-C939` · Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C688](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) · Used by `DEV-IMG-08`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Version 20 of the Screaming Frog SEO Spider, released in May 2024, was the first that could connect the crawler to ChatGPT through custom JavaScript, which let SEOs rewrite image alt text at scale.
  <br><sub>`D2-C946` · Day 2, Lightning session F: Media (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** To test LLM-generated alt text before a rollout, a community speaker recommended running the crawler's custom JavaScript in Screaming Frog's List mode on a few chosen URLs and reviewing the generated alt text, instead of crawling the whole site in Spider mode.
  <br><sub>`D2-C949` · Day 2, Lightning session F: Media (speaker not identified) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-IMG-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker cited W3C guidance that, when cleaning a transcript, it is usually not appropriate to correct the speaker's grammar or other mistakes.
  <br><sub>`D2-C955` · Day 2, Lightning session F: Media (Patrick Domanico) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google annotates each page with only one language in the index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C586` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Server location is not really a reliable country-targeting signal nowadays, so Google does not use it much; the recording is unclear on the word 'server'.
  <br><sub>`D2-C592` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google usually understands non-English words typed 'in English' (probably meaning romanised, Latin-letter spellings, which the speaker did not spell out); the speaker said this belongs to query interpretation, a Day 3 (serving) subject.
  <br><sub>`D2-C599` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D2-C965](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) · Extended by [D3-C051](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Whether machine-translated content is acceptable depends on the case and is the site owner's decision, after weighing three things machine translation can miss: translation quality, local conventions and cultural adaptation.
  <br><sub>`D2-C608` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-INT-10`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Localisation should account for local conventions such as date formats, which differ between Europe, the UK, the US and other countries, and calendars (in Thailand the current year is 2569), or a date can point users to the wrong day.
  <br><sub>`D2-C610` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-INT-10`, `DEV-SDA-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** According to the speaker, shoppers in Europe and the US pay a lot of attention to promotions and discounts when deciding to buy (no source for this was captured), one of the cultural factors localisation should take into account.
  <br><sub>`D2-C613` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** According to consumer data shown on a slide in the talk (source not captured), US consumers judge product quality more by user feedback and reviews, while European shoppers seem to look more at brand reputation.
  <br><sub>`D2-C614` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C341](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** According to consumer data shown on a slide in the talk (source not captured), German shoppers also rely heavily on expert recommendations and certifications when judging product quality.
  <br><sub>`D2-C615` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** According to consumer data shown on a slide in the talk (source not captured), French shoppers particularly want to know where a product comes from.
  <br><sub>`D2-C616` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker cited a Semrush study that found at least one hreflang error on 75% of multilingual websites; the study, reported in February 2017, audited 20,000 sites with several language versions (the speaker recalled it as about five years old).
  <br><sub>`D2-C633` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (Alizée Baudez) · not in Google docs · [75% of Multilingual Websites Have Hreflang Implementation Mistakes](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/75-multilingual-websites-hreflang-implementation-mistakes/185737/)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Arabic and Persian contain letters that look identical to users but are different characters to software, with different Unicode code points; the example given was the letter ye, which has an Arabic and a Persian form.
  <br><sub>`D2-C644` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Because Arabic and Persian lookalike letters have different code points, a searcher may type one variant of a word while a website's text uses the other.
  <br><sub>`D2-C645` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Lookalike Arabic and Persian character variants cause problems for data analysis and keyword research: data for one term can be split across the variants, which makes keyword research less accurate.
  <br><sub>`D2-C646` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Persian and Arabic are written right to left and English left to right, so a title that mixes the two scripts can display in a confusing, unpredictable order even when its content is correct.
  <br><sub>`D2-C963` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-INT-12`, the glossary term *Bidirectional text*</sub>

- **[Stage]** The display problem of mixing right-to-left and left-to-right text also affects product titles and URLs, the presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said, showing an example from a large Iranian e-commerce site.
  <br><sub>`D2-C964` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs · Used by `DEV-INT-12`, the glossary term *Bidirectional text*</sub>

- **[Stage]** The presenter of the non-Latin-script talk said that in competitive Persian, Turkish and Arabic searches, bought backlinks and paid editorial content still visibly influence rankings and are widespread (an observation; no data was shown); the presenter stressed this described the situation and was not a recommendation.
  <br><sub>`D2-C967` · Day 2, Lightning session G: Internationalisation (a second community speaker) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Smaller languages have fewer documents on the web and so worse coverage, from an indexing perspective, than large ones, for example Basque compared with Spanish or Portuguese, Hungarian compared with German, and Sicilian compared with Italian.
  <br><sub>`D2-C650` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google detects the language of each document and weights language in index selection so that the index is not dominated by one or two languages.
  <br><sub>`D2-C651` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C585](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Without language or country input to index selection, Google's index would become an English index, because so many documents on the web are in English.
  > "if you just let the index decide what to rank without language or country input, then you would have an English index"
  <br><sub>`D2-C652` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google also takes country into account in index selection, so that countries producing less content in a shared language, such as the UK for English or Switzerland for German, are not disadvantaged against the US or Germany, which produce most of it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C653` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Freshness plays no big role in index selection: whether a page was published 30 years ago or today makes no difference to its chance of being indexed.
  > "It doesn't play a big role in index selection."
  <br><sub>`D2-C658` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Whether a page's content is explicit does not matter for indexing: judged on content type alone, an explicit page has the same chance of being indexed as a major news site's homepage.
  <br><sub>`D2-C661` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google calculates SafeSearch signals during indexing rather than in ranking, because ranking happens online with no time for such calculations, while indexing has the processing power.
  > "In ranking, everything has to happen online, and there's just not enough time to calculate those things."
  <br><sub>`D2-C662` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** SpamBrain, Google's AI-based spam detection system, is nowadays built on Gemini and fine-tuned specifically for finding spam.
  > "built on top of, well, nowadays, Gemini, and fine-tuned to that specific purpose of finding spam"
  <br><sub>`D2-C669` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C041](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Extends [D1-C039](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by the glossary term *SpamBrain*</sub>

- **[Stage]** SpamBrain was said to detect 5 times more spam sites than the spam algorithms Google had launched before it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C673` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google gives two reasons for not indexing every URL it knows: most of them would not be useful to users, and including URLs in the index that users would never see would be an immense investment.
  <br><sub>`D2-C681` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection aims to index only documents that are useful to users now or potentially in the future.
  <br><sub>`D2-C683` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection is a predictive AI system that relies heavily on machine learning.
  <br><sub>`D2-C684` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C037](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection uses what Google already knows about a site: if the site, or even a section of it, satisfies users' needs well, new URLs from it are treated more forgivingly.
  > "the index selection system is going to be more forgiving when it sees a new URL from your site"
  <br><sub>`D2-C685` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C094](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-URL-10`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection uses the signals calculated earlier in indexing for each document it has to select or discard.
  <br><sub>`D2-C687` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C205](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by the glossary term *Index selection*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Index selection is the last step before documents enter Google's index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C688` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C026](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) · Extends [D1-C211](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by the glossary term *Index selection*</sub>

- **[Stage]** When Google's coverage of a country is limited, index selection becomes more likely to select documents relevant to that country, even if other signals would suggest otherwise.
  <br><sub>`D2-C689` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** When Google lacks content in a language, such as Basque, index selection becomes more likely to select lower-quality documents in that language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C690` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Under-served languages were presented as an opportunity: where Google's index holds a lot of spam in a language such as Basque, a site that starts publishing in that language can very likely replace that spam with its own content and rank for those keywords (one clause of the reasoning was inaudible).
  <br><sub>`D2-C691` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** The overall importance of a document or site plays a significant role in index selection.
  <br><sub>`D2-C693` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** News sites were given as the example of importance at work in index selection: they are generally very important on the web and their pages usually get indexed very fast ('indexed' is a likely but not certain reading of the recording).
  <br><sub>`D2-C694` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** 'Discovered – currently not indexed' in Search Console is a crawl-scheduling state: Google knows the URL exists but does not want to crawl it yet. Of the two not-indexed statuses discussed, it was called the 'kind of nastier' one.
  > "The first one is kind of nastier."
  <br><sub>`D2-C706` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C097](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extends [D1-C065](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`, the glossary term *Discovered – currently not indexed*</sub>

- **[Stage]** 'Crawled – currently not indexed' is most of the time a quality issue rather than a technical one: the pages are usually low quality or useless for the index, for example duplicates or soft 404s.
  > "most of the time it is actually a quality issue"
  <br><sub>`D2-C714` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C098](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** The first thing to check for pages reported as 'Crawled – currently not indexed' is whether their quality is on par with the parts of the site that Google does index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C715` · Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's Search index stores the tokens produced by tokenizing each page, as they are, together with the metadata attached to the tokens during tokenization.
  <br><sub>`D2-C720` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Repeats [D2-C323](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Used by `DEV-HTM-07`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's Search index does not hold the full content of pages; Google said storing full pages and pulling them out at serving time would be a very inefficient way of doing search.
  > "we don't have the full content of the page in our index"
  <br><sub>`D2-C721` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Repeats [D2-C318](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The snippet shown for a web result is reconstructed from the tokens stored in Google's index: Google knows the position of each token in the document and rebuilds the snippet from those positions.
  > "the snippet that you see was reconstructed from these tokens"
  <br><sub>`D2-C724` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C316](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said posting lists, which Google's serving system uses to find the pages that contain a query's words, are not new: they are at least 60 years old (as of 2026).
  <br><sub>`D2-C824` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C732](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For most of the tokens Google finds on the web, though not every single one, the index keeps a posting list of the URLs that contain that token.
  <br><sub>`D2-C733` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Repeated by [D3-C074](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Used by the glossary term *Posting list*</sub>

- **[Stage]** In posting-list retrieval, the posting lists of the query's words are intersected, which yields an unranked list of candidate URLs.
  <br><sub>`D2-C736` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C075](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Used by the glossary term *Posting list*</sub>

- **[Stage]** A search query is broken into words with the same segmenter or tokenizer that Google used to build the index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C737` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Repeats [D2-C321](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Extended by [D3-C013](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** At retrieval, Google looks up the posting lists of the query words that are actually important rather than of every word in the query.
  <br><sub>`D2-C738` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C075](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said a vector space also holds embeddings for associations the web makes with a page, such as what is known about its author; most of them sit far from typical queries, and a query that names the association may move closer to them.
  <br><sub>`D2-C744` · Day 2, How does the index look like? (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** The legacy Google Trends Explore page is still available but will be retired: Google is adding its features to the new Explore page until everyone can move to the new one (no date was given).
  > "the legacy Explore page, which is still available, but not for a long time"
  <br><sub>`D2-C763` · Day 2, Google Trends (Omri Weisman) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google Trends Explore chart presented on stage put worldwide search interest in Gemini above ChatGPT for the first time ever in September 2025, during a sharp surge for Gemini.
  <br><sub>`D2-C769` · Day 2, Google Trends (Omri Weisman) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google attributed the September 2025 surge in worldwide search interest for Gemini to the viral launch of Nano Banana (the image editing model in the Gemini app), as people searched for both Gemini and Nano Banana.
  <br><sub>`D2-C770` · Day 2, Google Trends (Omri Weisman) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C162](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** After the Nano Banana surge faded, worldwide baseline search interest in Gemini stayed much higher than before, which Google read as a sustained gain in brand recognition.
  <br><sub>`D2-C773` · Day 2, Google Trends (Omri Weisman) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google Trends chart of worldwide search interest in AI from 2004 to mid-2025 showed a huge rise in the two to three years before mid-2025.
  <br><sub>`D2-C776` · Day 2, Google Trends (Omri Weisman) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said worldwide search interest in AI has climbed far higher since mid-2025, beyond the range of the 2004 to mid-2025 chart shown in the talk.
  <br><sub>`D2-C827` · Day 2, Google Trends (Omri Weisman) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** An early-2012 worldwide spike in Google Trends search interest for 'ai' was caused by the global hit song 'Ai Se Eu Te Pego', whose title contains the Portuguese word 'ai', not by interest in artificial intelligence.
  <br><sub>`D2-C777` · Day 2, Google Trends (Omri Weisman) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A Google Trends engineer found the cause of the 2012 'ai' spike by zooming in on that time range on the Explore page and reading the related queries.
  <br><sub>`D2-C778` · Day 2, Google Trends (Omri Weisman) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Worldwide Google Trends search interest for ski since 2004 shows strong seasonality, peaking every winter.
  <br><sub>`D2-C782` · Day 2, Google Trends (Omri Weisman) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Worldwide Google Trends search interest for ski also shows a mostly steady decline since 2004, which can be misread as falling search volume.

- **[Stage]** Google said its internal numbers show the actual volume of ski-related searches is going up, even though ski's share of all searches in Google Trends has declined since 2004.

## Day 3 — Serving: Ranking, Search Console, and Performance (2026-10-02)

| Status | Claims | Meaning |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Confirmed | 103 | The documentation says the same thing |
| Consistent | 183 | The documentation supports it without stating it directly |
| Not in docs | 139 | Said or shown at the event, by Google or a community speaker, but not in Google's documentation |
| Not checkable | 102 | Nothing to verify: quotations, framing, agenda facts, audience questions, opinions |

### Said at the event but not in Google's documentation

These are the most valuable and the most fragile claims: quote them as "said at Search Central Live", not as documented policy.

- **[Stage]** Google named Thai as a language that makes query understanding more complex because it does not separate words with spaces; the speaker added, hedging with 'apparently', that Thai uses spaces to separate sentences.
  <br><sub>`D3-C011` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C320](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** After detecting the query language and separating the words, Google removes words it thinks matter little to the query, such as 'a' and 'of', known as stop words.
  <br><sub>`D3-C012` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Query understanding*, the glossary term *Stop words*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's query processing deliberately mirrors indexing: a query is transformed into something that can be matched against the index, and stop word removal is part of that transformation.
  <br><sub>`D3-C013` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C321](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) · Extends [D2-C737](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** For some searches the stop words are important, and Google then tries to recognise the whole phrase, stop words included, as an entity; in indexing, such words are indexed together.
  <br><sub>`D3-C014` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Stop words*</sub>

- **[Stage]** When a query names an entity, Google treats it as a request for that entity rather than as a collection of separate words.
  <br><sub>`D3-C016` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Query understanding*</sub>

- **[Stage]** In ranking, Google can match a query's words or its entity, and, the speaker said with a 'probably', mixes both to some degree.
  <br><sub>`D3-C017` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** In Google's example, the query word 'photograph' could be expanded to 'image', 'picture' or 'photo', but one German candidate had to be dropped because the similar German word means 'photographer', so expansions are language-specific.
  <br><sub>`D3-C019` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** For technical terms, Google's synonym swapping can return either a technical page or a simplified page for the same query.
  <br><sub>`D3-C022` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google suggested a test: a search that lists a term's synonyms joined with OR will probably return results very similar to the plain query, because Google adds the synonyms itself (part of the sentence is unclear in the recording).
  <br><sub>`D3-C026` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Internally, a short query can turn into a much longer rewritten query, because Google adds entities, synonyms and other information before looking it up.
  <br><sub>`D3-C029` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** In Google's rewrite example, [fried chicken place in Barcelona] keeps 'fried' and 'chicken' as two words, may add an entity for fried chicken, and replaces 'place' with alternatives such as 'area', 'location' or 'restaurant'.
  <br><sub>`D3-C030` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Some alternatives in a rewritten query make no sense, such as 'fried chicken area in Barcelona', which is harmless because few indexed pages match them.
  <br><sub>`D3-C031` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** In a rewritten query, a place name such as Barcelona can stay a word or be swapped for an entity, possibly a more specific location.
  <br><sub>`D3-C032` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Some synonyms are contextual and depend on the rest of the query: 'GM' probably means General Motors in [GM car], general manager in [GM restaurants] and genetically modified in [GM barley].
  <br><sub>`D3-C034` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's synonyms need not be synonyms linguistically: words people use interchangeably are treated as synonyms, because the aim is to find the right content in the index.
  > "we don't need to be technically accurate"
  <br><sub>`D3-C036` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Synonyms and siblings*</sub>

- **[Stage]** When Google highlights a word in its results that looks like the wrong synonym, the reason is probably that many people use the two words interchangeably.
  <br><sub>`D3-C037` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Besides synonyms, Google detects 'siblings', words in the same category that are related but not interchangeable, such as Canon and Nikon.
  <br><sub>`D3-C038` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Synonyms and siblings*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Because Canon and Nikon are siblings rather than synonyms, a search for [Canon camera] should not show Nikon cameras.
  <br><sub>`D3-C039` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Synonyms and siblings*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google learns synonyms and siblings from search behaviour: words people search with in the same way become synonyms, while frequent comparison queries mark words as not interchangeable (the end of the sentence is unclear in the recording).
  <br><sub>`D3-C040` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** To check whether Google treats two terms as the same, search for each: [Iberico ham] and [jamón ibérico] both brought up the same entity, so Google understands them as the same thing.
  <br><sub>`D3-C043` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** At the time of the talk, a search for [Spanish cured ham] brought up mainly a Wikipedia page, showing that Google does not automatically equate that phrase with Iberico ham.
  <br><sub>`D3-C045` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google sometimes gets diacritic variants wrong, so it is worth searching to see whether Google understands a variant; if it does, pick one spelling and use it.
  <br><sub>`D3-C049` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Users expect content written the way they search: in some languages they search in Latin characters, in others in the local script, and Hindi users, for example, search both in Hindi and in Latin letters.
  <br><sub>`D3-C051` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (John Mueller) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C599](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) · Used by `DEV-INT-11`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said a short video showing how one query is expanded into several fan-out queries has been in its documentation for a while.

- **[Slide]** Google's summary slide on query understanding said Google's synonyms are not always language-based; on stage this was explained as words people use interchangeably counting as synonyms even when they are not synonyms linguistically.

- **[Stage]** At retrieval, Google splits the query into words, applies query understanding and expansion, and matches the words and their expansions against the posting lists.
  <br><sub>`D3-C075` · Day 3, Making sense of users' queries (Gary Illyes) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C736](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Extends [D2-C738](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Used by the glossary term *Retrieval*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Because a query like [best fried chicken ever] can match millions of pages, Google already orders the candidates during retrieval, before ranking starts.

- **[Stage]** Google's research on how AI changes consumer purchase decisions, presented in October 2026, was based on 23,000 conversations with consumers (the talk did not say in which countries).

- **[Stage]** Because people do not always do what they say they will do, Google's research on AI and purchase decisions also analysed panels with 40,000 participants, together with research partners, besides the consumer conversations (the talk did not make clear whether 40,000 is one panel or the total).
  <br><sub>`D3-C554` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's headline finding was that people who use AI features such as AI Mode or AI Overviews feel much more confident about their purchase decisions.
  <br><sub>`D3-C557` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's research found that consumers delegate the mental effort of a purchase decision to AI without surrendering the choice itself, which Google calls being 'boosted'.
  > "that doesn't mean they are surrendering their choices. What's happening is that consumers are feeling boosted."
  <br><sub>`D3-C559` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Boosted consumers*</sub>

- **[Stage]** According to Google's research, AI turns consumers who were confused and overwhelmed by information and options into consumers who feel empowered, like category experts, and able to make the best purchase for their needs.
  <br><sub>`D3-C560` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** The first benefit consumers get from AI, according to Google's research, is ease: AI synthesises information quickly into an easy-to-digest form and makes choice overload manageable, so consumers can offload cognitive effort.
  <br><sub>`D3-C561` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Boosted consumers*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's research also counted easy access as part of AI's ease benefit: multimodal input, such as taking pictures, and low friction lower the barrier to entry.
  <br><sub>`D3-C562` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C018](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The second benefit, assistance, is that AI reduces a complex category, such as smartphones or trip planning, to the few features that really matter (for a phone, the battery and the picture quality), so consumers feel like experts.
  <br><sub>`D3-C563` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Boosted consumers*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Assistance also includes showing consumers what people in similar situations chose, because people are social and want that reassurance (the wording of this passage is partly uncertain in the recording).
  <br><sub>`D3-C564` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's research found that consumers who do not use AI pinball between exploration and evaluation, while AI users start a purchase journey mostly exploring and then move on to evaluating, a path that looks more like a funnel.
  <br><sub>`D3-C566` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** The third benefit, suggestion, is that AI often proposes ideas, brands and products a consumer had not thought of, which lowers the cost of curiosity.
  <br><sub>`D3-C568` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs · Used by the glossary term *Boosted consumers*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's research found that people who use AI also visit more brand websites, because it is simply easier.
  > "the people that are using AI, they search more, and they also visit more websites of brands."
  <br><sub>`D3-C571` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C005](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** AI users sometimes take even longer purchase journeys, but they perceive their journeys as shorter, a perception the data does not always support (part of this passage is uncertain in the recording).
  <br><sub>`D3-C573` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** For high-risk or high-involvement purchases, ease, assistance and suggestion are often not enough, and consumers add a reassurance step to reduce the risk of the decision.
  <br><sub>`D3-C574` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** After exploring with AI, people often go back to Google Search and to the websites of the product or service providers to double-check before buying, for example trust in the company and cancellation policies.
  <br><sub>`D3-C575` · Day 3, Mastering the messy middle (Pablo Pérez, Senior Marketing Research & Insights Manager) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** A new or less familiar brand should expect people to double-check it and should prepare assets that give them the extra reassurance they need at that last step.
